key_insight: LLM-as-judge bias is not just an input-output glitch; it also shows up in the model’s hidden representations. The paper finds a representation-level explanation of judge unfairness that helps explain why different bias types persist across many judges and benchmarks.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the challenge of understanding and mitigating scoring bias in LLM-as-judge systems beyond prompt-level or input perturbation analyses. It aims to explain where bias lives inside the model and how to diagnose it more directly.
method: Analyzes hidden-state geometry of judge models to identify how biased and unbiased inputs are represented internally.
Compares seven judges across seven bias types and nine benchmarks to test whether representation-level patterns generalize.
Connects mechanistic interpretability findings to practical bias mitigation and judge evaluation strategies.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides a deeper diagnostic lens for evaluating LLM judges and designing better safeguards. It can improve trust in automated evaluation systems by revealing when score bias is rooted in internal representations rather than only in prompts.
visual_elements: A side-by-side diagram of input-output bias analysis vs. hidden-state representation analysis
A geometry plot showing clustered judge inputs in activation space
A heatmap comparing bias strength across seven judges and seven bias types
An interpretability pipeline graphic from prompt input to internal representation to final score
paper_title: Inside the Unfair Judge: A Mechanistic Interpretability Account of LLM-as-Judge Bias
paper_authors: Zixiang Xu, Sixian Li, Huaxing Liu, Xiang Wang, Shuai Li
